abstract: A student fluent in German is needed for the Fall 2008 to search German and Austrian press and literature for references to and opinions about Czechoslovakia and Poland, especially in regards to the treatment of the Sudeten and other eastern Germans before and after the war. This is for an article that I am writing on the place of Czechs and Czechoslovakia in the German narrative of suffering. It is my contention that Czechs play an outsized role in German memories of the war because, unlike the Poles, the Czechs can be cast as perpetrators of unjustified crimes against the Germans. In German eyes, the Czechs "had it good" during the war and therefore Czechoslovakia had no justification for the expulsion of the Sudeten Germans afterwards. (German exiles by contrast prefer not to talk about what happened in Poland during the war, thereby implicitly recognizing some justification for the expulsion from the "recovered territories.") The result is a particularly potent narrative of Sudeten German martyrdom that posits Germans as victims and not merely perpetrators of the Second World War. It's a narrative that still complicates international relations today.

title: Crumbs of Fresh Bread for Everyone: Mexican Rural Women and the Reconstruction of Community
abstract:
In the half century between 1880 and 1930, Mexican rural peoples entered into migratory agricultural work. In the larger context of twentieth-century North American history, the formation of this migratory work force was a crucial element in the making of two modern economies. Some of this is well studied. But several pressing issues remain. First, historians know remarkably little about how the rural poor actually confronted the changes that engulfed their communities. Second, they have little studied how the rural poor reconfigured and reconstituted communities in the face of physical and cultural dismemberment. Third, historians still lack a full understanding of the ways that migration facilitated the recovery of rural communities. And, finally, far too little of the work that does exist on these issues is comparative. This project aims to speak to these issues through a historical study of women and men in northern Mexico and the Southwestern United States between 1880 and 1930. More specifically, my work seeks a historical understanding of womens reconstitution of rural communities: of their provisioning activities in sustaining their households and kin; of their reconstructing their communities in the face of disruption; of their entry into migratory work; and of their capacity to act collectively to reconstitute networks and communities at home and abroad.

In my research thus far, I have uncovered much documentation in northern Mexican and US Southwestern repositories, public and private, local, state, and national. I am pro;posing to employ a Leopold Fellow to work through the inventories and documents in two enormous collections on 20th-century American labor: the AFL-CIO archives at the State Historical Society at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and the CIO Secretary-Treasurer's archives at the Walter Reuther Library at Wayne State University. Both collections have printed and on-line inventories; both have microfilm editions of about half of the documents. The Leopold Fellow's research will have both a general thrust -- the labor-movement context of women's movements in the US Southwest -- and a specific focus -- the local efforts at women's unionization that stretch from 1907 to the early 1940s. Since both the AFL-CIO and the CIO Secretary-Treasurer's collections are immense, the Fellow's work will require both creativity and perseverance. In addition, the Fellow's work will require a week's visit to Madison and a week in Detroit, to read the large cache of relevant files not yet microfilmed. Along the way, the Fellow will acquire many research skills, much knowledge about the Mexican and US borderlands, and, perhaps, develop a topic for independent research. If the Center will consider summer work, as the announcement contemplates, I would very much like the student to begin in July or August.

abstract:
The project in question is an edition of letters written by and to the noted historian Ernst Kantorowicz (1895-1963). The edition in turn would help serve as a basis for a biography of Kantorowicz that I am ultimately planning. My projected edition would draw on letters in public collections as well as on a considerable number that are in my possession. Kantorowicz, a German emigre who taught at Berkeley (1939-1950) and then was located at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton until his death in 1963, is widely recognized as one of the most important and influential historians of the twentieth century, above all for his seminal book, The King's Two Bodies. In addition he was an important figure in American academic life as a result of his being one of the leaders of the opposition to a McCarthyite loyalty oath at Berkeley, which resulted in his dismissal. His letters contain references to his role in the loyalty oath crisis and the writing of his major work; they also refer to current politics and very often are devastatingly witty.

Research Assistant Responsibilities: The letters contain many references to the work of other scholars, and sometimes to current events that are not immediately easy to identify. All such references will need annotation, and I need a good research assistant to help with this job. The work would consist of looking up data in biographical repositories, historical surveys, and sometimes locating articles in journals to which Kantororowicz is referring. Some knowledge of German would be a plus because Kantorowicz frequently alluded to work in that language. But this is not an absolute requirement. It is too early to tell whether any travel would be necessary, but checking regional university archives (especially those of the University of Chicago) for hitherto unnoticed letters by Kantorowicz would not be out of the question.

title: Small Business in Poor Urban Communities
abstract: The work to be done arises from my current research on nineteenth-century “slum” communities and bridges into work that I plan to undertake in the future. The student researcher will use statistical, library, and archival resources to study the lives of immigrant and African American small business persons in poor areas of Chicago and Cincinnati in the mid-nineteenth century. The student will begin by doing some basic reading about these communities, in both secondary works and in the manuscript I am writing. Then, using materials I have already gathered, together with information from the Northwestern and other area libraries, the student will undertake a study of one or perhaps two wards in the cities mentioned above. He or she will create collective biographical databases (prosopographies) containing basic census information from 1860 about all of the immigrant and African American individuals who own real estate and are engaged in low-level entrepreneurial work (storekeepers, saloonkeepers, coal dealers, boarding house keepers, laundry owners, etc.). The student will then look for these individuals in other kinds of records — tax lists, property deeds, directories, political and legal records -- expanding the collective biography to allow an examination of careers. The researcher may need to spend a few days in Cincinnati to access records only available at the Cincinnati Historical Society and the Hamilton County Courthouse. The overall goal will be to trace the lives of these individuals backward and forward in time, asking how they acquired property and how their situations changed, and comparing people of different backgrounds, men and women, residents of different places. I will help the student to use this information to address larger questions: What role did small stakeholders from minority backgrounds play in the larger political and social life of their cities? To what extent did property give them leverage, either formal or informal? How did they make use of the ward-based political systems then dominant in these cities? How did they engage with the powerful business and political leaders of the civic elites? To what extent did these obscure entrepreneurs shape the physical and social development of the city? The student will conclude the work by writing a report on his/her findings. I will work closely with the student at all stages of this process.

title: The Unknowns: Skepticism in Early Modern Venice
abstract: I will be pursuing a research project on a Newberry Library Fellowship during the academic year 2008-2009. The project involves analyzing a group of thinkers who in early seventeenth century in Venice took advantage of the absence of press censorship to popularize a strain of religious and philosophical skepticism, which, I want to argue, directly influenced the Enlightenment thinkers of the eighteenth century. The central figures in promoting skeptical thought in Venice were the members of the Academy of the Unknowns, a debating society whose members published hundreds of books and pamphlets over a thirty year period, many of which were translated from Italian into French and English. The Unknowns, pioneers in what we would now call journalism, created an engaging literary style in their novels and histories that were intended to arouse passionate emotions rather than to convince through reason, a trait that helps account for their widespread influence at the time but also for the fact that their appeal is easily lost on modern readers. This project intends to recapture the world of the Unknowns, to analyze their writings, and to evaluate their appeal during the early modern period. I am looking for a student who has a very good command of Italian to help with reading and taking notes on some of the more than 150 books by members of the Unknowns available in Chicago. A considerable number of them are in the Northwestern University Library Rare Books collection, which is where the student will work. Since I will be working at the Newberry, I will be able to supervise the student on a regular basis.

title: Ukrainian Jewish poet in Soviet newspapers of the 1930s and 1940s
abstract: I am looking for a student competent in Russian (strong readings skills would suffice) for one quarter in 2009-2010. My project is a follow-up to my recently published book "The Anti-Imperial Choice" (Yale University Press). One of the main characters of my book, the enigmatic Ukrainian Jewish avant-guard poetess Raisa Troianker (1909-1945) contributed to both Russian and Ukrainian belles lettres. Her two books of Ukrainian verse introduced Jewish themes, urban futuristic motifs, and sexual imagery into Ukrainian poetry. While her Ukrainian contribution has been covered in my chapter, her experience as a Russian cultural figure, quite significant, has not. Between 1935 and 1945, Raisa Troianker worked as an editor, columnist, and poet-in-residence for the daily "Poliatnaia pravda" (Polar Circle Truth), the Murmansk-based most important newspaper in the north-western part of the Soviet Union. This newspaper acquired special importance after the Nazi invasion of the USSR in 1941. Troianker was known to have spent weeks in the trenches near Murmansk and to have written first-hand reports for this newspaper. Besides, she appeared in it with her short stories and poetry. I am working on a bilingual (Russian-Ukrainian) edition of Troianker's works and need a Russian-competent student to go through the microfilm reels of the "Poliarnaia pravda" newspaper, find, catalogue, and collect Troianker's texts (including dubbia). In addition to providing a candidate with solid background in the Soviet Union history in mid-twentieth century, I will train him/her in bibliography, communication and propaganda, and archives.

title: Marketplace Solutions: Southern Segregationists and the Surprising Career of School Vouchers
abstract: I am seeking assistance for my current book project, “Marketplace Solutions”: Southern Segregationists and the Surprising Career of School Vouchers. The story begins with the closure of the public schools in Prince Edward County, Virginia, from 1959-64, an outgrowth of southern segregationists’ policy of “massive resistance” to Brown v. Board of Education which included the first modern tuition grants (i.e. school vouchers). Scholars of civil rights have depicted the school closures as the twilight of massive resistance, but what I’ve found in the archives is, rather, the dawn of the era of privatization, often described as “neo-liberalism.” The book examines the learning process through which southern conservatives arrived at privatization as a way to insulate privilege from the mass democratization of the era, and charts the coalition building that altered national discussion and policy. The research follows the southerners' discovery of allies in the northern- and western-based nascent conservative movement, their alliance-building with proponents of libertarian economics (above all, the founders of public choice economics and law and economics), and their contributions to the “original intent” constitutionalism that later flowed into the Federalist Society and related efforts. The book will also chart their involvement with new institutional partners such as the American Enterprise Institute, the Republican Party, and later, the Heritage Foundation. And it examines their efforts to cultivate ties between evangelical Protestants and Catholics over voucher advocacy. I would like the assistance of a Leopold Fellow for varied research tasks, but will probably the student’s core research focus will likely be the story of Milwaukee, home to both the oldest and largest voucher experiment in the country and longtime Catholic voucher advocacy. The Leopold Fellow would carry out this work, ideally, during Winter, Spring, and perhaps also Summer, or during Spring and Summer quarters. Applicants must have expertise in EndNote by the time they start work, and possess outstanding research and writing skills as well as initiative and reliability. No language ability required, although Spanish would be a plus. Time: ideally Fall, Winter, Spring, or Spring and Summer quarters.

title: Chinese Modernity
abstract: I would like to request the assistance of a Leopold Fellow for the entire 2009-2010 academic year. The student would need to read Chinese fluently. The Leopold Fellow would assist me with two research projects: 1) the location and preparation of primary materials to support the translation into Chinese and publication of my 2006 Stanford University Press book, Between Heaven and Modernity: Reconstructing Suzhou, 1895-1937, by the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, and 2) research assistance for my ongoing book project, “’This Time of Suicide’: Modernity, Society, and Self in China, 1900-1957.” Between Heaven and Modernity examines the transformation of urban space in late 19th and early 20th c. Suzhou by analyzing the experience of various people, including the poor, elite gentry, Japanese monks, central state officials, foreign and domestic tourists, and local businessmen, as city leaders attempted to modernize the city. The book was awarded the Best Book (Non-North American) by the Urban History Association in 2007. A Leopold Fellow would help identify, copy, and collate primary sources—and perhaps help with other relevant research tasks—for the preparation of the Chinese translation. My current book project analyzes the changing significance of suicide as a social phenomenon in China from the late Qing dynasty, through the Republican period, until the end of the initial years of stability that followed the founding of the People’s Republic. During this period, China was gripped by a series of social panics regarding the prevalence of suicide in urban society. Concern over suicide as a malady of modernity were key to the reconceptualization of the populace as “modern society,” the production of new forms of social knowledge such as sociology, vital statistics, and medicine, and the growth of governmental power. Debates on suicide also both helped precipitate and reflect shifts in overall assumptions regarding gender, the power of society, and the autonomy of the individual. The book documents the powerful influence of social science on the Chinese state and society during several decades of reformist and revolutionary ferment. A Leopold Fellow would help identify relevant materials in Republican era newspapers and journals, both of which are essential primary sources for this project.

title: Edition and Study of a Fourteenth-Century Treatise
abstract: I am currently editing and commenting on a Latin treatise concerning the Great Schism of the West (1378-1416) that was written in 1385. The basis for my project is that I have discovered a hitherto unknown manuscript copy of the treatise that dictates the necessity of a critical edition. (An edition based on a poorer manuscript copy was brought on in 1909.) Moreover, the treatise itself is an important neglected source: it was written by an author very close to the scene of the contested papal election of 1378. Although this author is avowedly partisan, he presents a very vivid narrative of events, full of circumstantial details, that has never been weighed sufficiently by modern scholars. Thus the purpose of the project is not only to offer a new edition but to vindicate the value of the treatise. title: The Italian Renaissance: The Virtues of Doubt/Local Knowledge
abstract: I would like a Leopold Fellow to assist me in researching my new book project. This is a book that aims to provide an overview of the Italian Renaissance that breaks with old conventions. The book opens unconventionally with an examination of religious expression in all its forms and ends with religious skepticism and, even more unconventionally for a study of the Italian Renaissance, the rise of commercial theater. That introduction and conclusion signal a distinctive approach to the period, which has usually been framed by political events and secular intellectual movements such as humanism. One of the lasting achievements of the Italian Renaissance was the creation of a powerful if elite culture that prized skepticism and anti-clericism within a regime of hegemonic Catholicism. It is also a period in which the liturgy of the Church neither declined nor disappeared, in contrast to much of northern Europe, but was reinvigorated and reasserted in highly theatrical forms that paralleled the rise of the new non-liturgical theater of commedia dell’arte and grand opera. The Italian Renaissance, it is argued, provoked neither the rise of secularism nor the decline of religion. Anti-clericism and even philosophical atheism became distorted mirror images of the triumphant Roman Church. These tensions between the Church Triumphant and its critics can serve as a metaphor for a broader set of contradictions that help explain the creative dynamism of Italian Renaissance society. An important running argument of the book is that social and ideological frictions stimulate doubt, a virtue that is the source of new ideas. title: Registering Birth: Populations and Personhood in the United States of America
abstract: This research project (and, ultimately, book) traces the practice of recording birth from the early national period through the mid-twentieth century, examining the multiple and often overlapping reasons for (and methods of) tracking when, where, and to whom, babies were born. At the beginning of the nation, nonstate recording practices were both more immediate and more widespread than was official birth registration. Using a diverse array of sources, the project will explore how and why families recorded births in bibles and diaries, plantation owners tracked the growth of their slave population, doctors kept private records – and sometimes registered – the births they attended, and churches recorded birth and baptism. Gradually, however, governmental registration supplemented and then supplanted local and informal practices. This shift was neither accidental nor inevitable. Rather, birth registration was the object of reformist attention and its ubuiquity the fruit of considerable labor. By the mid-1930s, the effort to achieve full registration had been largely successful. States reformed their laws governing vital statistics collection, medical professionals and parents absorbed the notion that a birth was of interest to the government, and a variety of public and private institutions began to rely on the birth certificate as the foundational affixation of identity. A Fellow would help with two distinct research tasks. First, the Fellow would travel to Washington, D.C. to use archival records from the Children’s Bureau located in the National Archives. Second, the fellow would conduct magazine and newspaper research in Evanston to help identify significant events, legal reforms, and persons involved in the history of birth registration.

title: George Washington and the Creation of American Nationalism
abstract: Almost as soon as he became President of the United States, George Washington set off on a long trip of extraordinary significance for the nation. During the fall of 1789, he traveled from New York, then the capital of the new republic, to the modern state of Maine. And then, during the spring of 1790 he took a more ambitious journey from New York to Georgia. In the tradition of Early Modern European monarchs who organized "progresses" throughout their kingdoms, Washington planned a "republican progress." Aware from the battle over the ratification of the Constitution that the American people were deeply divided, he understood almost intuitively that he represented the hopes for the country, and by visiting thousands of ordinary men and women he aimed to set his own unifying figure against the divisive local interests that threatened the republican experiment. In this sense, he possessed in the fullest sense what Max Weber meant by charisma. A Leopold Fellow assisting me would trace Washington's journey, noting in scattered town histories and regional newspapers how his appearance affected the political culture. The student should possess basic research skills and familiarity with the interpretation of primary sources.

title: Small Business in Poor Urban Communities
abstract: The work to be done arises from my current research on nineteenth-century slum communities and bridges into work that I plan to undertake in the future. The student researcher will use statistical, library, and archival resources to study the lives of immigrant and African American small business persons in poor areas of Chicago and Cincinnati in the mid-nineteenth century. The student will begin by doing some basic reading about these communities, in both secondary works and in the manuscript I am writing. Then, using materials I have already gathered, together with information from the Northwestern and other area libraries, the student will undertake a study of one or perhaps two wards in the cities mentioned above. He or she will create collective biographical databases (prosopographies) containing basic census information from 1860 about all of the immigrant and African American individuals who own real estate and are engaged in low-level entrepreneurial work (storekeepers, saloonkeepers, coal dealers, boarding house keepers, laundry owners, etc.). The student will then look for these individuals in other kinds of records tax lists, property deeds, directories, political and legal records -- expanding the collective biography to allow an examination of careers. The researcher may need to spend a few days in Cincinnati to access records only available at the Cincinnati Historical Society and the Hamilton County Courthouse. The overall goal will be to trace the lives of these individuals backward and forward in time, asking how they acquired property and how their situations changed, and comparing people of different backgrounds, men and women, residents of different places. I will help the student to use this information to address larger questions: What role did small stakeholders from minority backgrounds play in the larger political and social life of their cities? To what extent did property give them leverage, either formal or informal? How did they make use of the ward-based political systems then dominant in these cities? How did they engage with the powerful business and political leaders of the civic elites? To what extent did these obscure entrepreneurs shape the physical and social development of the city? The student will conclude the work by writing a report on his/her findings. I will work closely with the student at all stages of this process.

abstract: I’m beginning work on a new project about the history of the U.S.-Mexico border since World War II, and I would like a Leopold Fellow to help me during its early stages of development. Rather, it has remained a hodgepodge of rivers, barbed wire, steel walls, observation towers, customs houses, international gateways, and works of art. My project will be about the construction of these various materials that make up the border. In one sense, by writing this history of the construction of the modern border, I aim to critique work on the border and borderlands that has approached these subjects rather imprecisely. But Im also interested in writing a comparative history of several border cities, something that historians have not done before. I would like help collecting newspaper articles from U.S. and Mexican border cities, as well as in identifying state and national archival materials in both the United States and Mexico, which contain information about the construction of the border. This work will involve searching online databases, and may require the Leopold Fellow to correspond with archivists and librarians.

title: Biography of Eminent Historian Ernst Kantorowicz

people.school: WCAS and Bienen School of Music

abstract: I am in the midst of writing a biography of Ernst Kantorowicz (1895-1963), an important German-American intellectual. Kantorowicz was one of the greatest medieval historians of the twentieth century: his biography of the Emperor Frederick II (1927) was one of the most widely-discussed books of Weimar Germany, and his The King’s Two Bodies (1957) has influenced work in numerous disciplines and remains one of the best-selling works in history more than half a century after its publication. Kantorowicz by no means only just sat at his desk. Quite to the contrary, he had an extremely eventful, often turbulent career. He fought in the First World War (battle of Verdun; Turkish front), and then in 1919, as a far-rightist, against the “reds” in Berlin and Munich. Until 1933 he belonged to the elitist circle of the charismatic poet, Stefan George. Although a rightist, he was an ardent anti-Nazi and spoke against them courageously from the lecture platform in 1933. Then he was forced out of his professoriat, and emigrated to the U.S. In 1939 he gained a position at the University of California, Berkeley. By then he had moved to the left and in 1949/1950 he was one of the leaders of opposition to a loyalty oath imposed on the Berkeley faculty. Because he refused to sign the oath he was fired. Then he spent the final part of his career at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. His Anglophone friends and correspondents included Maurice Bowra, Isaiah Berlin, Felix Frankfurter, J. Robert Oppenheimer, and George Kennan.
